item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 4: From Silos to Value Streams: How AI Rewires the Org Chart
item.description: Episode 5 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 4 opens Part II, "The Seven Shifts," with the first shift: Functions to Flow. After Part I's three models (the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree), Kersten argues that organizing around functional silos stops working when AI extends everyone's reach across domains. We cover handoffs and wait states, Priceline's drop from fifteen handoffs to five, and the Dedicated Leadership Model, Amazon's Single-Threaded Owners and Leaders, and single-, dual- and triple-leader structures. We also cover Kersten's claim that AI makes single leaders viable in more cases. Then value stream scope and "independence of action," SLAs for supporting functions, Value Stream Management and its lean manufacturing roots, capacity-based funding, and Weighted Shortest Job First. Finally, the TUI Group case: flow time cut from two hundred days to fifteen, a four-level AI literacy ladder, more than three thousand internal agents, and managers moving from owning people to owning outcomes. item.title: Building AI Native: Rethink Everything: When Agents Write the Code, Every Rule Breaks
item.description: A pilot of Building AI Native, a builder-to-builder show for engineers making AI-native products. We dig into Avi Flombaum's essay series "Rethink Everything": the claim that most software best practices were optimizations for a human programmer who no longer writes the code. We cover verification over line-by-line reading, one-shot rewrites against end-to-end tests, choosing languages by strength rather than familiarity, small services in one repository with deliberate duplication, owning your infrastructure, and types as agent feedback. Then the tradeoffs: comprehension debt, slow end-to-end suites and the identity question. We close with one experiment to try this week. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 3: The Outcome Tree: Scaling AI-Era Orgs Like Redwoods, Not Waterfalls
item.description: Episode 4 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 3, "The Outcome Tree," is the last of Part I's three foundational models, after the Product Operating Model and the Outcome Loop. We also cover the short Conclusion to Part I, which previews the book's seven shifts. Kersten's question is how to scale one Outcome Loop to hundreds or thousands of value streams. We cover the "AI in Waterfall" dysfunction, the coordination math (n times n minus one connections), matrix overlays, Kotter's "second operating system," Holacracy and Haier's RenDanHeYi, and Geoffrey West's sublinear and superlinear scaling. We also cover the nature behind the model: redwoods, fractals, insulin and abscisic acid. Then the tree itself, with value streams as leaves, MECE partitioning, objective and budget cascades, and branching factors. Finally, Kersten's own path from Xerox PARC and AspectJ to building the Outcome Tree at Tasktop with help from Adrian Cockcroft and the Reverse Conway Maneuver, and his speculative idea of "organization as code." item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 2: The Outcome Loop: Constraints, AI Surplus, and the Next Bottleneck
item.description: Episode 3 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 2, "The Outcome Loop," sits in the middle of Part I, "Outcome Management." It builds on Chapter 1's Product Operating Model, sets up Chapter 3's Outcome Tree, and is the core model that the book's seven shifts in Part II build on. Kersten defines the loop as the feedback system that connects inputs (strategy and budget) to outputs (activities and artifacts) to outcomes (employee, customer and business) and back again. We cover production elasticity and Amazon, the lineage from outcome-based healthcare and Jobs to Be Done to OKRs, Kersten's own path from PhD research to Tasktop, key results versus KPIs, the TeenWellness worked example, why the loop is a hypothesis test, broken telemetry and the "counting procedures" trap, applying the Theory of Constraints, and how the VS Code team's bottleneck moved from delivery to onboarding to code review as AI took over more of the output. item.title: From AI Skeptic to Agent Whisperer: Rethinking the Work
item.description: Mitchell Hashimoto's essay "My AI Adoption Journey" traces a measured path from AI skeptic to working with an agent alongside them most days. We cover Mitchell's three phases of adopting any tool (inefficiency, adequacy, discovery) and their six steps: dropping the chatbot for tool-using agents, doing the work twice to learn what agents do well, end-of-day agents for a "warm start," outsourcing the slam dunks with notifications off, "harness engineering" with AGENTS.md and verification tools, and always having an agent running. We also cover the open question Mitchell raises about skill formation, especially for juniors. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 1: AI Won't Fix Your Company If the Bottleneck Isn't Code
item.description: Episode 2 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 1, "Product Operating Model," opens Part I, "Outcome Management," and is the first of the book's three foundational models, before the Outcome Loop (Ch 2) and the Outcome Tree (Ch 3). Kersten argues that AI's tenfold boost to coding won't help companies whose bottleneck sits elsewhere. In his State of the Industry data, only 8% of the time from idea to running software went to building it. We cover the Theory of Constraints and the jammed on-ramp, the history from McCallum's org chart to Gantt charts, Snowden's Cynefin framework and when to run a project versus a product, irreducible uncertainty and where AI can augment but not replace decisions, Reinertsen's life cycle profitability, the operating-model dysfunctions in Kersten's reports, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia's path from project to product to AI-native engineering. item.title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean: Inside the Interpretability Reversal
item.description: When a neuron seems to respond to unrelated things, is the network a tangled knot, or have we just not figured it out yet? We dig into Nick Cammarata's Goodfire essay 'Neural Networks Are Already Clean,' which argues superposition should be the last explanation, not the first. Along the way: the cat-and-car neuron that was really a V detector, layers squeezed from 480 neurons to 10 that got coarser instead of tangled, the Santa answer that lived on neurons' negative side, a neuron that tracks Colorado, attribution graphs up to trillion-parameter models, and the essay's speculative case for spotting deception hiding in plain sight. item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 0: When AI Removes the Bottleneck: From Outputs to Outcomes
item.description: Episode 1 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 0, "Foundations," comes after the Preface, Prompt and Introduction and before Part I's three models: the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree. Kersten argues that AI is making knowledge output nearly free, which moves the bottleneck from producing work to the organization itself. We cover the productivity paradox, the Theory of Constraints (and the car-plant paint shop), the earlier shift to software as a service, Carlota Perez's model of technological revolutions and her "golden age," the "three million Shakespeare plays" problem, and Kersten's account of Cognition's weekly outcome loop, where it throws away much of its code. We also cover the risk he warns about: AI's gains piling up in a few giants. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: Code Is Cheap, Attention Isn't: Inside Agentic Code Review
item.description: When AI agents write code faster than any human can read it, review becomes the bottleneck. This deep dive walks through a new pattern-language paper by Davis, Gill, Hendrickson, Jones, Ma, Shoup and Wickett (Enterprise Technology Leadership Journal, Fall 2026). It argues that human review survives because of trust, compliance and accountability, and should give way to a layered verification stack: cheap automated checks, review depth set by risk, and decision records you can audit. We cover nine patterns, from small incremental changes and context engineering to adversarial AI review and teams of specialist review agents. Then come three real deployments: Block's agent-written changes that nobody felt they owned, Cloudflare's 131,246 review runs averaging about 1.2 findings each, and DryRun Security's tenant-isolation lesson. We finish at the speculative edge, the "dark software factory," where humans become curators of knowledge rather than reviewers. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: When AI agents outrun the org chart, the bottleneck moves
item.description: When AI agents finish the backlog faster than a company can plan, where does the work get stuck? Mik Kersten's keynote "Output to Outcome: When Agents Outrun the Org Chart" argues the bottleneck moves from output to the operating model itself. We cover the theory of constraints, a pattern across technological revolutions, and the parable of Peerless Auto putting an electric motor on an old drive shaft. We also go through Kersten's figures: teams use only about 8% of delivery time, TUI Group cut idea-to-customer time from about 200 days to 15, and Cognition's Devin reportedly throws away far more code than it ships. Then the proposed fix (the outcome loop, the outcome tree, AI-native SAFe and human ownership of every outcome) and the strongest objections the IntuiBloom graph raises. item.title: Beyond Faster: How AI Can Expand What You Dare to Do
item.description: Felix Rieseberg, who works on Claude, wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with AI models. Following an IntuiBloom graph of the essay, we walk through its four kinds of ambition: speed, altitude (aiming at the outcome, like replacing a quarterly deck), depth (expert instruments, raw data, an outside judge) and range (assembling a cross-field crew, methods not costumes). We cover the data and tools these need, then the psychology of why we hold back: self-efficacy, hard goals, Dantzig's "homework", the four-minute mile and permission to fail. item.title: Cancer's Second Verb: Converting Tumors Instead of Killing Them
item.description: A walk through a knowledge graph built from Brian Roemmele's X post on a KAIST study (Advanced Science, 2024). As the post tells it, researchers built a 'digital twin' of an intestinal cell's gene network, used an algorithm called BENEIN to pick three genes (MYB, HDAC2, FOXA2), and turned colon cancer cells into normal-like cells in cell lines and mice by maturing them rather than killing them. This is early preclinical work with no human data, described secondhand, and nothing here is medical advice. The graph adds context: differentiation therapy has treated the leukemia APL for decades, the idea builds on Waddington, Kauffman and Yamanaka, and hard-to-drug targets, durability (speculative) and the tumor's surroundings could keep it from becoming a therapy.
